title: The obvious lookup is the trap, not the tool
explanation: `getent passwd 1301` (and `id 1301`, and `ls -l` on any file with that owner) returns exactly one name. NSS's UID lookup (`getpwuid()`) has no concept of "there might be more than one account at this number" — it just returns the first `/etc/passwd` entry that matches and stops. It will confidently show you `logshipper` even when the file in question actually belongs to `metricsagent`.

title: See both entries by reading the file, not looking one up
explanation: `awk -F: '$3==1301 {print}' /etc/passwd` scans every line instead of resolving a single number, and reveals both `logshipper` and `metricsagent` claiming UID 1301. This is the only reliable way to detect a duplicate UID — any tool that does a keyed lookup by definition can't show you a collision.

title: As far as the kernel is concerned, they are the same identity
explanation: File ownership, permission checks, and process credentials are all UID-number based — the kernel doesn't track usernames at all. `metricsagent` and `logshipper` aren't two accounts that happen to overlap; for every permission decision the kernel makes, they're one and the same principal, which is why this is a real identity-confusion bug and not just a cosmetic `ls -l` quirk.

title: Renumber the newer account, not the one with real data
explanation: `logshipper` already owns production data at `/var/lib/logship/data`; `metricsagent` was the one created later with a stale next-free-UID calculation. Fixing the account that's actually wrong — rather than picking whichever is more convenient — avoids having to untangle ownership on files that were already correct.

title: usermod -u re-chowns what it already knows the account owns
explanation: `sudo usermod -u 1302 metricsagent` updates the account's UID and automatically re-chowns files still tagged with its old UID that it can find (like its own home directory) — no separate manual `chown` pass needed for those. `logshipper` and its data were never touched, since they were correct the whole time.

title: Verify with the same read-the-file approach, not a single lookup
explanation: `id logshipper` and `id metricsagent` should now report different numbers, and `awk -F: '{print $3}' /etc/passwd | sort | uniq -d` should come back empty — confirming no duplicate UID remains anywhere, not just that these two specific accounts look fine.
